opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's helpful to set it against the dominant view. Most of today's AI follows what I'd call connectionism: you build a huge network, feed it lots of data, and trust that the right behavior emerges from the connections. That's been enormously successful, but it treats the model as a black box. It's essentially "scale is all you need."

Structuralism starts from a different belief: that intelligence, and the world it models, has structure. There are symmetries, modularity, compositionality, hierarchies, sometimes even simple symbolic laws. If that structure is really there, we shouldn't make the network rediscover it from scratch with brute force. We should find ways to discover it, expose it, and build it into the learning process.

So when I think about AutoRL, or automating research more broadly, my question isn't just "how do we make the agent bigger and train it longer?" It's "what structure does this problem have, and can the system learn that structure explicitly?" Can it find the right decomposition of a task, the right inductive biases, the reusable modules? If it can, you get several things together: much better data efficiency, better generalization outside the training distribution, and interpretability, because the structure is something a human can actually look at and understand.

That ties into my earlier work, like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. The motivation there was the same: build models whose internal structure can line up with the structure of the problem, so in the best case you can read a formula out of the network instead of just a pile of weights.

I'm not saying connectionism is wrong. Scale clearly works. But I think the next step is to pair scale with structure. Connectionism gives you the power, and structuralism gives you the understanding, and ideally the efficiency too. That's why I use the word: it's a stance that the structure of things matters, and that our AI systems should be built to find it, not just absorb it.

fable-5.1.text:
I use the word structuralism because I think the dominant way people approach reinforcement learning right now is, in a sense, empiricist. You collect a lot of data, you build a big model, you let gradient descent find whatever it finds, and you hope the structure emerges on its own. And sometimes it does. But what I care about is the opposite direction: starting from the structure of the problem and asking what the learning system should look like given that structure.

If you look at my background, I came from physics and from interpretability work, and the thing physics teaches you is that the world is not a pile of unrelated facts. There are symmetries, conservation laws, hierarchies, compositional pieces that fit together in specific ways. When I look at an RL problem, I see the same thing. A task has a decomposition. It has subgoals that relate to each other in a graph-like way. It has invariances, things that shouldn't matter to the policy. Structuralism, for me, means treating these relationships as the primary object, and treating the parameters as secondary.

So in AutoRL, instead of automating hyperparameter search, which is what a lot of the field has meant by the word, I'm trying to automate the discovery of structure. Can the system figure out how a task decomposes? Can it figure out which parts of the state space are actually relevant, and which representation makes the problem simple? Once you have that, the learning problem itself often becomes much easier. Sometimes almost trivial. The hard part was never fitting the function. The hard part was knowing which function to fit.

There's also a philosophical reason I like the term. In linguistics and anthropology, structuralism was about the idea that meaning comes from relationships between elements rather than from the elements themselves. I think that applies to intelligence too. A good policy isn't good because of the particular numbers in its weights. It's good because it encodes the right relationships between states, actions, and outcomes. If we can make those relationships explicit, we get something that's more interpretable, more transferable, and honestly more scientific. You can look inside and understand why it works, rather than just observing that it works.

So that's the bet. Structure first, then learning. Not the other way around.

astra-6.text:
I call it structuralism because the emphasis is on the structure of the learning process. In reinforcement learning, you have a policy, an objective, an update rule, and an interaction with the environment. Those pieces are usually designed separately, with a lot of human judgment built in.

The way I think about AutoRL is to ask: which relationships are essential, and which choices can themselves be learned? Once you define a structure, you can let an automated process search within it. But that structure already determines what the system can discover.

So automation doesn’t eliminate the need for design. It moves the design problem up a level—from choosing a particular algorithm to choosing a space of possible algorithms. That shift is what I mean by structuralism.

sol-6.1.text:
I call it structuralism because I’m interested in the structure behind a learning algorithm, rather than treating the algorithm as a fixed recipe and just tuning its parameters. In AutoRL, the question becomes: what are the components, how do they interact, and which of those choices can themselves be learned or searched over?

That changes how you think about automation. You’re not simply asking a machine to find a better learning rate. You’re asking it to explore a space of possible learning rules. But defining that space already introduces assumptions, so the structure we give the search is very important. Too restrictive, and we can only rediscover what we already know; too unconstrained, and the search becomes very difficult.

So, for me, structuralism means trying to identify the right building blocks and relationships—the structure that makes discovering a new algorithm possible.
